children: KKR is creating a new equipment-finance company Akrapoint Commercial Capital with an initial investment of $350 million.

Akrapoint expects to issue loans that help small and medium-size businesses finance mission-critical equipment across the "mid-ticket" range, which it defines as $250,000 to $5 million in cost. The company foresees the average loan being around $500,000 to $600,000.

"We believe there's a real need in this mid-ticket space that they're going to serve, where it's focused on vocational assets, specialty trailers and other industrial equipment," said Daniel Pietrzak, the global head of private credit for KKR.
The Denver-based company, which is majority owned by KKR, will finance equipment across a range of U.S. industries, including manufacturing, energy, sanitation and waste services.
"Akrapoint will offer both a loan and a lease product," Pietrzak said. "It'll likely be more loans than leases, but like most equipment businesses out there, the company will offer both."
The average duration for one of these loans will be five years with amortizing terms.

KKR believes there are a number of themes driving demand for essential equipment, including reshoring of manufacturing and a broader push to invest in critical infrastructure, a spokesperson for the firm said.

Meanwhile, traditional lenders continue to retreat from this type of business, creating an opportunity for new entrants with the right expertise and capital to scale, the spokesperson added. Banks are still the dominant provider of capital to the equipment-finance market, but they are losing share because they are not participating in the sector's growth for various reasons, including regulatory standards that require them to maintain a certain amount of liquid capital.
Akrapoint Commercial Capital is starting with 20 employees, but the company expects to expand its team as underwriting and originations grow.

Akrapoint is led by Chief Executive Nate Smith, who spent nearly a decade at commercial equipment financing and leasing company Trans Lease, where he oversaw credit, portfolio management, funding and compliance.
Gary Shivers, a founder of Navitas Credit Corp. who has 30 years of equipment and other finance experience, will chair Akrapoint's board of directors.

KKR is funding the Akrapoint investment out of its second asset-based finance fund, KKR Asset-Based Finance Partners II, which closed in 2025 with $6.5 billion. KKR has already deployed most of the fund across 25 transactions, including one with Harley-Davidson that reduced $450 million of the company's debt and returned nearly $500 million to shareholders.

KKR has also backed other asset-based finance deals from various investment pools, including $500 million in debt financing for HarbourView Equity Partners, an asset manager focused on investment opportunities in entertainment, media and sports.
The firm also entered an agreement with PayPal to purchase up to EUR65 billion, or $74.56 billion, of current and future buy now, pay later loans originated in Europe through March 2028.

KKR's overall asset-based finance group has amassed $92 billion in assets under management since 2016, with roughly 60 people dedicated to the strategy. The firm's ABF strategy focuses on mortgage finance, commercial finance, hard asset-backed loans and contractual cash flow loans.
